newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council divided on Iraqi disarmament goals.
newsitem.headline: UN Council divided on Iraqi disarmament goals.

text.p: Four Security Council members on Friday criticized a report from Rolf Ekeus, in charge of Iraqi disarmament, saying he needed to give Baghdad a more detailed list of what was left to be settled.

"There is a request for more detailed information as to what remains to be done, specifically," Russia's ambassador Sergei Lavrov told reporters. He said France, Egypt and China had raised similar criticisms.

Ekeus, head of the U.N. Special Commission in charge of ridding Iraq of weapons of mass destruction, briefed the Security Council on his week-old report that said Iraq still had not come clean on weapons materials under its control.

A clean bill of health by the commission is a key requirement before the embargo on Iraqi oil exports can be lifted entirely. Iraq has been under U.N. sanctions since its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.

But the United States' representative, Karl Inderfurth, supported Ekeus' report saying his details of harrassment of inspectors by Iraqi officials represented a "step backwards" from Iraq's earlier commitments, a U.S. official said.
Washington, he said, believed Iraq still had some operational Scud missiles and there were "very good odds" that some of them carried biological and nerve-agent warheads.

Ekeus himself has made similar assertions, saying the commission still did not have enough information to make sure Iraq has eliminated its weapons capabilities or at least submitted them to monitoring.
Russia, China and France have all recently signed oil exploration deals with Iraq that await the lifting of sanctions before they can be implemented.
Lavrov said also questioned Ekeus' assertion that "a small number" of governments had not responded to repeated and long-standing requests for information.
Ekeus' report said it would be "most unfortunate" if this prevented the commission from being able to give Iraq clearance required for any lifting of sanctions.
Lavrov told reporters he did not believe Iraq could be blamed for what information governments did not supply.
In response, Ekeus told reporters that information from governments would make life easier for the commission but that it could continue its work without it.
